cities.base: The wedge between the Plaza, Canyon Road and the Railyard. Stay inside it and you walk to the museums, the galleries and dinner without moving the car once. Cerrillos Road motels are half the price an
cities.name: Santa Fe

cities.base: Within a few blocks of Taos Plaza, ideally on the north side toward the Taos Inn, so the Pueblo is ten minutes away and you can walk to dinner. Anything out on Paseo del Pueblo Sur past the Ranchos tu
cities.name: Taos

cities.base: The Abiquiu Inn on US 84 at the village, or a plain room in the Ghost Ranch casitas thirteen miles further north. Ghost Ranch puts you inside the landscape at first light, which is the entire point of
cities.name: Abiquiu

cities.base: Old Town or the Los Ranchos strip along Rio Grande Boulevard, both close to the river path and to the good cheap food. Nob Hill along Central works if you want to walk to a bar at night.
cities.name: Albuquerque

cities.base: No beds worth taking. This is the loop you drive out of Santa Fe: up to Bandelier, over the Jemez Mountains through the Valle Grande, down the Jemez River past Soda Dam, and back to I-25 by Cochiti. S
cities.name: Bandelier, Los Alamos and the Jemez

cities.base: There is no lodging, no food, no fuel and no cell signal in the canyon, and the only beds are tent and RV sites at Gallo Campground. Come in from US 550 at Nageezi on CR 7900: eight miles paved, then
cities.name: Chaco Canyon

places.name: Santa Fe Plaza and the Palace of the Governors Portal
places.note: The vendors under the portal are Native artists juried into a programme run by the Palace of the Governors, selling their own work at fixed spots drawn by lottery each morning, so this is the one place on the Plaza where the prices are fair and the provenance is real. Ask before photographing anyone

places.name: New Mexico History Museum and the Palace of the Governors
places.note: The Palace is the oldest continuously occupied public building in the country and the museum behind it does the 1680 Pueblo Revolt properly rather than as a footnote. Open daily May through October; closed Mondays November through April, which catches people out.

places.name: Museum of International Folk Art
places.note: The Girard Wing is 10,000 objects in one room and it is the best hour in Santa Fe if you let it be. Daily May to October, Tuesday to Sunday November to April, and free docent tours at 10:30, 11:30 and 2.

places.name: Georgia O'Keeffe Museum
places.note: Small, crowded and worth an hour, but the paintings make sense only after you have stood in the Chama badlands, so go here after Abiquiu rather than before. Book online; walk up tickets sell out in summer.

places.name: Canyon Road
places.note: About eighty galleries in half a mile of adobe, ranging from serious contemporary work to bronze coyotes in bandanas. Most open at ten and many close Sunday and Monday; Friday evening openings put wine in your hand and take the edge off the retail.

places.name: Santa Fe Farmers Market
places.note: Saturday all year and Tuesday in the growing season, in a permanent hall in the Railyard. Late August through September is chile roasting season and the smell of the drum roasters in the parking lot is the single best argument for coming in autumn.

places.name: Loretto Chapel
places.note: You pay to file past one spiral staircase in a deconsecrated chapel while a recording tells you a carpenter story with no documentary basis. Walk two blocks to San Miguel Chapel instead, which is genuinely one of the oldest church structures in the United States and costs a dollar.

places.name: Meow Wolf House of Eternal Return
places.note: A two storey walk through installation inside a former bowling alley, made by a Santa Fe artist collective and still the best of the several they now run. Loud, dark, full of children, and about ninety minutes longer than most adults want. Timed entry, book ahead.

places.name: Ten Thousand Waves
places.note: A Japanese style bath house in the pines fifteen minutes up toward the ski basin, with a communal tub and a row of private ones. Reservation only and worth booking the day you land. The izakaya downstairs does a good three course lunch for about thirty dollars.

places.name: The Shed
places.note: Family run since 1953 in a 1692 adobe, and the red chile is the benchmark everything else in town gets measured against. Lunch is walk in only and the line forms before eleven thirty; dinner takes reservations. Order the red, get the posole, and know that Christmas means both chiles.
places.neighborhood: East Palace Avenue, half a block off the Plaza

places.name: Horseman's Haven Cafe
places.note: A diner in a petrol station on the ugly end of Cerrillos Road serving the hottest green chile in Santa Fe. There is a level one and a level two; the level two is not a joke and they will ask if you are sure. This is where locals eat and no one is performing anything.
places.neighborhood: Cerrillos Road, at the Giant station

places.name: Sazon
places.note: Fernando Olea cooks moles here and has done for decades, and the mole tasting is the one expensive dinner in Santa Fe that is about a cook rather than a view. Reserve well ahead. If it is full, Paloma on Galisteo does the same idea for two thirds of the money.

places.name: Taos Pueblo
places.note: Visitors are welcome, on the community's terms. Roughly a thousand years of continuous occupation, no electricity or plumbing inside the old walls, and about 150 people living in them now. Photography of the village is allowed for personal use but absolutely never inside San Geronimo Chapel, never o
places.neighborhood: Taos Pueblo, two miles north of the Plaza

places.name: San Francisco de Asis Church
places.note: Finished in 1816 and re-mudded by the parish every June, which is why it still looks like that. Walk round the back first: the buttressed apse is what O'Keeffe painted and Ansel Adams photographed, and the front is the dull side. It is an active parish, so Sunday mornings belong to the congregation.

places.name: Millicent Rogers Museum
places.note: A Standard Oil heiress's collection of Navajo and Pueblo jewellery, Hispanic devotional art and the Martinez family blackware from San Ildefonso, which is the best single room of pottery in the state. Closed Mondays in the off season; call in winter.

places.name: Harwood Museum of Art
places.note: The Taos Society of Artists downstairs and the Agnes Martin octagon upstairs, seven pale paintings in a room built for them, which is the reason to come. Opening days have moved around in recent years, so check before walking over.

places.name: Rio Grande Gorge Bridge
places.note: 650 feet of air under a steel deck over the Rio Grande, and the walkways out to the mid span belvederes are the whole visit. Trucks make the deck move. There are crisis line phones on the rail, which tells you something, and vendors in the west lot most mornings.

places.name: Earthship Biotecture Visitor Center
places.note: Off grid houses built from rammed earth tyres and bottle walls, a whole subdivision of them on the mesa, and you can walk through one model. Half serious architecture and half 1970s true belief, and better in person than it sounds.
places.neighborhood: US 64, Tres Piedras side of the gorge

places.name: Wild Rivers Recreation Area, La Junta Point
places.note: The rim above where the Red River drops into the Rio Grande, with a stepped trail 800 feet down to the confluence. The descent takes forty minutes and the climb back takes an hour in full sun. Carry two litres each, there is no water at the bottom.
places.neighborhood: Rio Grande del Norte National Monument, north of Questa

places.name: Williams Lake Trail
places.note: Four miles round trip to a cirque lake at 11,040 feet under Wheeler Peak. The distance is nothing and the altitude is everything, so do not put this on day one. Afternoon thunderstorms in July and August are reliable enough to set a watch by, so be off the top by noon.

places.name: Black Rock Hot Springs
places.note: Two rock pools at the river's edge at the bottom of a dirt switchback road, reached by a ten minute scramble. Free, clothing optional, and underwater whenever the Rio Grande runs high in spring melt. The road is unsuitable for a low rental car after rain.
places.neighborhood: Rio Grande gorge below Arroyo Hondo

places.name: Orlando's New Mexican Cafe
places.note: A small bright room and a patio, no reservations, and a queue at the door from noon. Get the Los Colores plate and the carne adovada. The green here is hotter than the red, which is the opposite of the usual.
places.neighborhood: Don Juan Valdez Lane, north Taos

places.name: The Love Apple
places.note: Twenty five seats by candlelight in a deconsecrated 1800s chapel, cooking local and organic without making a speech about it. Reservations are essential and are taken weeks out in summer. Check the payment policy when you book, they were cash and cheque only for years.
places.neighborhood: Paseo del Pueblo Norte, in the old Placitas chapel

places.name: Adobe Bar at the Taos Inn
places.note: Taos calls it the living room of the town and that is roughly accurate. Free live music most nights under a skylit adobe ceiling, a decent margarita, and a crowd that is half visitors and half people who have been coming for thirty years.
places.neighborhood: Paseo del Pueblo Norte at the Plaza

places.name: Georgia O'Keeffe Home and Studio
places.note: The adobe compound she bought as a ruin in 1945 and spent twenty years rebuilding, including the studio window that frames the view in painting after painting. Small guided groups leaving from the welcome centre on US 84, booked weeks ahead in summer, tour season roughly March to November. No photog

places.name: Chimney Rock Trail, Ghost Ranch
places.note: Three miles round trip and about 600 feet up a steep sandy shoulder to a mesa edge looking down the Chama valley at Pedernal, the flat topped mountain O'Keeffe said God would give her if she painted it enough. No shade at all. Register at the welcome centre and pay the day use fee.

places.name: Box Canyon Trail, Ghost Ranch
places.note: Four flat miles up a cottonwood streambed into a red walled dead end where the canyon closes over your head. The easiest walk at Ghost Ranch and the one to do in the heat, since half of it is shaded and you cross running water.

places.name: Kitchen Mesa Trail, Ghost Ranch
places.note: Four and a half miles with a genuine scramble through a chimney in the caprock near the top, hands needed, and a mesa top afterwards that most people have to themselves. Not for anyone unhappy on exposed rock, and do not start it after nine in summer.

places.name: Ruth Hall Museum of Paleontology
places.note: One room, and in it a block of the Coelophysis quarry dug out of the hill above, which produced hundreds of Triassic dinosaurs and made this ranch a significant fossil site. Twenty minutes if you rush and an hour if a staff palaeontologist is in.

places.name: Plaza Blanca
places.note: White rock badlands eroded into fins and hoodoos, the White Place of the O'Keeffe paintings, sitting on land owned by the Dar al-Islam mosque. It is private property opened to respectful visitors: sign in at the trailhead, dress modestly near the mosque, and take nothing. Three miles of dirt road to

places.name: Echo Amphitheater
places.note: A natural sandstone half dome a five minute walk from a Forest Service car park, and it really does throw your voice back at you. Worth the twenty minute detour if you are driving north anyway, not worth a trip on its own.

places.name: Abiquiu Lake and the Pedernal view
places.note: A reservoir on the Chama with Cerro Pedernal standing behind it, and the view from the dam overlook at last light is the reason to sleep in Abiquiu rather than day tripping. Water levels swing hard with the snowpack so some years the boat ramps are dry.
places.neighborhood: Corps of Engineers dam overlook, NM 96

places.name: Monastery of Christ in the Desert
places.note: A Benedictine community at the end of thirteen miles of washboard dirt along the Chama, with a George Nakashima designed chapel and hours sung through the day that visitors may sit in on quietly. The road is the hard part and it is impassable after heavy rain. No phone signal, so decide before you t
places.neighborhood: Forest Road 151, up the Chama canyon

places.name: Bode's General Store
places.note: Petrol, fishing licences, hardware and a deli counter that makes the breakfast burrito everyone in the valley eats. It has been the only shop for miles since 1919 and it is where you buy lunch before a Ghost Ranch hike, because there is nothing else until Espanola.

places.name: Cafe Abiquiu at the Abiquiu Inn
places.note: The only proper dinner between Espanola and Chama, which is the honest reason to eat here, but the New Mexican plates and the patio under the cottonwoods hold up. Book if you are staying anywhere nearby, because everyone else has worked out the same thing.

places.name: Old Town Plaza and San Felipe de Neri
places.note: The 1706 Spanish colonial core, with the church on the north side still holding mass after three centuries. The plaza itself is ringed with turquoise shops selling a lot of imported silver, so go early, look at the adobe, and do not buy jewellery here without knowing what you are looking at.

places.name: Indian Pueblo Cultural Center
places.note: Owned and run by the nineteen pueblos themselves, and the correct first stop before you visit any of them. It is also where you learn which are open to outsiders and which are not: Taos and Acoma welcome visitors on tours, Walatowa at Jemez Pueblo is closed to non members year round and you see it o

places.name: Acoma Sky City
places.note: A village on a 367 foot mesa, occupied since at least the 1100s, and you can only go up on a guided tour from the Sky City Cultural Center below. Tours hourly from 9:30 to 3:30. Buy the still photography permit at the desk before you board the bus, expect video and drones to be refused outright, and
places.neighborhood: Acoma Pueblo, an hour west on I-40

places.name: Rinconada Canyon, Petroglyph National Monument
places.note: A two and a half mile sand loop along a basalt escarpment carrying several hundred images pecked into the rock, most of them made by ancestral Pueblo people between 400 and 700 years ago. Soft sand the whole way and no shade. These are sacred to the pueblos: look, do not touch, and do not chalk or w

places.name: Sandia Peak Tramway
places.note: Fifteen minutes and 4,000 vertical feet to a 10,378 foot crest, with the Crest Trail running along the top if you want an hour of walking up there. Go for sunset and watch the city lights come on. Closed Tuesdays, plus a maintenance shutdown most spring and autumn, so check the date.

places.name: Paseo del Bosque Trail
places.note: Sixteen miles of flat paved path under old cottonwoods along the river, with no road crossings on the whole length. Early morning it belongs to runners and roadrunners. Late October the cottonwoods turn and it is the best free hour in the city.
places.neighborhood: Rio Grande bosque, Central Avenue access

places.name: Anderson Abruzzo Balloon Museum
places.note: Better than it has any right to be: gas balloon crossings of the Atlantic and Pacific, Cold War spy balloons, and the physics of why this valley has a wind pattern that lets pilots steer. If you are here the first full week of October the Balloon Fiesta itself is on and everything in the city double

places.name: Mary and Tito's Cafe
places.note: A pink room on Fourth Street with a James Beard America's Classic award on the wall and the best carne adovada in the state. Order the stuffed sopaipilla with red. Closed Sundays and Mondays, cash preferred, and worth planning the day around.

places.name: The Frontier Restaurant
places.note: Open from five in the morning, cafeteria line, John Wayne paintings, and a student and shift worker crowd at every hour. Get the green chile stew, a breakfast burrito and one cinnamon roll to share, because they are the size of a paperback.

places.name: El Pinto
places.note: A 1,000 seat hacienda with gardens, a salsa brand and a coach park, and the food is fine and costs double what better food costs elsewhere in town. If you want a patio and a margarita go to Los Poblanos; if you want New Mexican food go to Mary and Tito's.

places.name: Campo at Los Poblanos
places.note: A 1930s John Gaw Meem ranch on twenty five acres of lavender and organic field, cooking what the farm grows. Expensive, and the setting is doing a lot of the work, but the bread and the field greens are real. Walk the lavender rows before dinner; they cut in July.

places.name: Sister Bar
places.note: A rooftop patio on Central and the most reliable live music room downtown, running from touring indie bands to local punk. Downtown Albuquerque at night is thin outside a few blocks, and this is one of them.

places.name: Pueblo Loop Trail and Alcove House, Bandelier
places.note: A mile and a half along the canyon floor past Tyuonyi and the cavate rooms carved into volcanic tuff, with short ladders up into the cliff dwellings. Alcove House adds four tall wooden ladders and 140 feet of exposed climbing to a ceremonial cave. Entry is 25 dollars a vehicle, cashless, and a free

places.name: Tsankawi
places.note: A mile and a half loop on an unexcavated mesa where the trail itself is the artefact, worn knee deep into the soft rock by centuries of feet, with three ladders and a village site nobody has dug up. Covered by the Bandelier pass. Almost always empty and better than the main canyon for it.
places.neighborhood: Detached Bandelier unit, NM 4 at White Rock

places.name: Falls Trail, Bandelier
places.note: Three miles round trip down canyon to an overlook above the Upper Falls, through the volcanic rock the whole plateau is made of. The trail below the overlook has been closed since the post fire floods and does not reach the Rio Grande any more, so turn around there.

places.name: Valle Grande, Valles Caldera
places.note: A fourteen mile wide grass floor inside a collapsed supervolcano, with elk on it at dawn and dusk and a short easy loop from the entrance station. No entrance fee. The vehicle gate is 9 to 5 most of the year and 8 to 6 in high summer, but you can walk in from the highway gates dawn to dusk.

places.name: Battleship Rock and McCauley Warm Springs
places.note: A prow of volcanic rock where two canyons meet, and a two mile climb from the picnic ground to a set of warm pools full of small fish that nibble. Around 85 degrees, not hot, and busy at weekends. Day use fee at the picnic area.

places.name: Soda Dam
places.note: A travertine mound built up over thousands of years by hot springs depositing calcium carbonate across the Jemez River, with the road blasted straight through it. Five minutes from the car, worth stopping for, not worth planning around.

places.name: Jemez Historic Site, Giusewa Pueblo
places.note: The ruins of the Giusewa village and the enormous 1620s San Jose de los Jemez mission church the Spanish made the residents build on top of it, told from the pueblo's side rather than the mission's. The descendants of the people who lived here are at Walatowa down the valley. Opening days shift, so

places.name: Walatowa Visitor Center, Jemez Pueblo
places.note: This is as close as an outside visitor gets to Jemez Pueblo, and that is the point. The village of Walatowa itself is closed to non members all year, so do not drive in to look. The centre has a small museum, a trail to a red rock overlook, and horno bread and fry bread stands outside on weekends.
places.neighborhood: Jemez Pueblo, NM 4 south of Jemez Springs

places.name: Jemez Springs Bath House
places.note: An 1870s stone bath house run by the village, with individual mineral tubs filled from the spring behind it. Plain, old and cheap, the opposite of Ten Thousand Waves. Book a slot by phone, because there are only a handful of tubs.

places.name: Slot Canyon Trail, Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks
places.note: Three miles through a slot narrow enough to touch both walls, then a steep 630 foot climb to a rim above the cone shaped tuff hoodoos. It sits on Cochiti Pueblo land, was shut from 2020 until late 2024, and now runs on timed entry reservations through Recreation.gov with a hard cap on numbers. No bo
places.neighborhood: Cochiti Pueblo land, off I-25 exit 259

places.name: Puye Cliff Dwellings
places.note: The ancestral village of Santa Clara Pueblo on a mesa above the Rio Grande, and the guides are Santa Clara people talking about their own ancestors, which makes it a very different visit from Bandelier. Guided access only, ladders on the cliff tour, and the pueblo closes it for ceremonial days. Ask
places.neighborhood: Santa Clara Pueblo land, NM 30 west of Espanola

places.name: Bradbury Science Museum
places.note: The national laboratory's own museum, free, with Fat Man and Little Boy casings and a defence gallery that is unmistakably the lab telling its own story. Useful and uncomfortable in equal measure. Opening days have changed more than once recently, so ring 505-667-4444 before making the drive for it.

places.name: Chaco Visitor Center
places.note: Pay the 25 dollar vehicle fee here by card, fill every water bottle you own, and use the toilets, because these are the last of all three in the park. Backcountry trail permits are free and self issued at the trailheads but the rangers here will tell you what is passable.
places.neighborhood: Park entrance, south end of the canyon

places.name: Pueblo Bonito
places.note: Around 600 rooms and 30 kivas in a four storey D shaped block, built in stages between roughly 850 and 1150 and laid out on a wall that runs true north and south. You walk through the interior rooms. Take the trail guide from the box and give it two hours, not forty minutes.

places.name: Chetro Ketl
places.note: The second great house, a quarter mile along the cliff from Pueblo Bonito on a paved path, with an elevated plaza built up on fill and a colonnade nobody has convincingly explained. Most visitors skip it, which is their loss. Walk between the two rather than driving.

places.name: Pueblo del Arroyo
places.note: A great house built out on the wash rather than against the cliff, with a tri walled structure at the back that has no clear parallel anywhere else in the region. Quieter than Bonito and a five minute walk from the same car park.

places.name: Kin Kletso
places.note: A compact rectangular great house in a later masonry style that points north toward Mesa Verde, and the start of the scramble up the cliff cleft to Pueblo Alto. Worth a look on its own and unavoidable if you are doing the mesa top.
places.neighborhood: Downtown Chaco, west end of the loop

places.name: Pueblo Alto Trail
places.note: Five miles on the mesa top reached by squeezing up a cleft in the cliff behind Kin Kletso, with the overlook straight down onto Pueblo Bonito and the traces of the prehistoric road system running off north. Free self issued permit at the trailhead. No shade, no water, and the cleft is a genuine scra

places.name: Casa Rinconada
places.note: The largest great kiva in the canyon, 63 feet across, standing alone on the south side with small village sites around it. Its north and south doorways line up almost exactly with true north. A short loop from its own car park across the wash.

places.name: Hungo Pavi
places.note: Largely unexcavated, which means you see the mounded shape of a great house rather than its rooms, and that is instructive after a morning inside Pueblo Bonito. Ten minutes from the road, usually nobody there.

places.name: Una Vida and the petroglyph trail
places.note: One of the three earliest great houses, begun around 850, mostly unexcavated, with a short spur up the rock to a panel of petroglyphs. It starts at the visitor centre car park, so it is the thing to do if the light goes before you get up canyon.

places.name: Penasco Blanco and the Supernova pictograph
places.note: Seven miles round trip up the wash to an oval great house on the west mesa, passing a pictograph of a star, crescent and handprint that many researchers read as a record of the 1054 supernova. Flat but long, entirely exposed, and impassable when the wash runs. Carry four litres each.
places.neighborhood: West end of the canyon, beyond Kin Kletso

places.name: Chaco night sky programme
places.note: An International Dark Sky Park with its own observatory and volunteer astronomers running telescope evenings around the new moon in the warmer months. The catch is real: you cannot be on that dirt access road after dark unless you are camping at Gallo, so this means a tent night.
places.neighborhood: Chaco Observatory, by the visitor centre

outings.why: The multi storey adobe blocks have been lived in for roughly a thousand years and people still live in them without electricity or running water inside the old walls. It is a village, not a site. The hard part is behaving like a guest: no p
outings.name: Taos Pueblo
outings.season: Year round except the roughly ten week winter quiet time and
outings.fallback: San Francisco de Asis at Ranchos de Taos and the Millicent Rogers Museum, which is where you go when the Pueblo is shut.

outings.why: Chimayo, Cordova, Truchas, Las Trampas and Peñasco, the Spanish land grant villages strung along the Sangre de Cristo foothills, ending in Taos. It is the drive you do once, northbound, with the car full. The road is slow and the santuario
outings.name: The High Road to Taos
outings.season: Year round, but the Truchas to Peñasco stretch ices over in
outings.fallback: The low road up NM 68 through the Rio Grande canyon at Pilar, 90 minutes and prettier than it has any right to be.

outings.why: Frijoles Canyon floor, the cavate rooms cut into ash tuff, ladders into the cliff dwellings, and then four wooden ladders and 140 feet of rock up to the Alcove House ceremonial cave. Straightforward walking, but the ladders are exposed and
outings.name: The Pueblo Loop and Alcove House at Bandelier
outings.season: Year round; Alcove House ladders close in ice
outings.fallback: Tsankawi on the way back, 90 minutes, unexcavated and almost always empty.

outings.why: NM 4 climbs out of Bandelier onto the rim of a fourteen mile wide collapsed caldera, drops through Battleship Rock and the red Jemez canyon, and ends at the ruined mission church at Giusewa. Mostly driving with four or five short walks. Do
outings.name: The Jemez loop: Valle Grande, Soda Dam and Jemez Springs
outings.season: Year round; NM 4 over the caldera can close for snow Decembe
outings.fallback: Valle Grande and the La Jara loop only, out and back, four hours.

outings.why: Chimney Rock is a steep 45 minute climb to a mesa edge looking straight down the Chama valley at Pedernal, and Box Canyon is a flat walk up a streambed into a dead end amphitheatre. Two very different hours. Register at the Ghost Ranch welc
outings.name: Chimney Rock and Box Canyon at Ghost Ranch
outings.season: Year round; avoid midday June through August
outings.fallback: Box Canyon alone, ninety minutes, level the whole way.

outings.why: The adobe compound she spent twenty years rebuilding, with the studio window that frames the view in half the late paintings. Small groups, booked weeks out in summer, and you see it on the guide's schedule not your own. No interior photogr
outings.name: The O'Keeffe Home and Studio tour in Abiquiu
outings.fallback: Plaza Blanca, the white rock badlands behind the Dar al-Islam mosque, ten minutes up the road and free.

outings.why: Six hundred rooms of coursed sandstone masonry laid to solar and lunar alignments, then a climb through a cleft in the cliff to look down on the whole thing from the mesa. The archaeology is extraordinary and the logistics are the problem:
outings.name: Chaco: Pueblo Bonito and the Pueblo Alto loop
outings.season: Year round, but only when the access road is dry
outings.fallback: The Downtown Chaco walk from the visitor centre to Pueblo Bonito and Chetro Ketl on the paved loop, three hours, no climbing.

outings.why: A village on a 367 foot sandstone mesa, occupied since at least the 1100s, reached only on a guided tour from the cultural centre below. Tours hourly from 9:30 to 3:30. Buy the still photography permit at the desk, leave the phone in the ca
outings.name: Acoma Sky City
outings.season: Year round except feast days, ceremonial closures and Christ
outings.fallback: El Malpais lava badlands and the Sandstone Bluffs overlook, forty minutes west.

outings.why: A narrow slot squeezing between pumice walls, then a steep scramble to a rim above the cone shaped hoodoos. It sits on Cochiti Pueblo land, reopened in late 2024 after four years shut, and now runs on timed entry reservations through Recrea
outings.name: The Slot Canyon Trail at Tent Rocks
outings.season: Year round when the pueblo has it open; book in advance
outings.fallback: The Pueblo Loop at Bandelier, which needs no reservation.

outings.why: Four miles round trip through spruce to a glacial cirque lake under Wheeler Peak at 11,040 feet. Modest on paper and hard on lungs if you flew in yesterday. Continuing to the Wheeler summit adds four hours and 2,000 feet.
outings.name: Williams Lake from Taos Ski Valley
outings.fallback: The Williams Lake trailhead loop or the West Rim Trail along the gorge, flat and at 7,000 feet instead of 11,000.

outings.why: The rim drive above the junction of the Red River and the Rio Grande, with a stepped 800 foot descent to the water if you want it. Going down is easy and coming up is an hour of switchbacks in full sun with no water at the bottom.
outings.name: Wild Rivers: La Junta Point and the Rio Grande confluence
outings.season: April to November; the rim road is plowed inconsistently in
outings.fallback: The Rio Grande Gorge Bridge overlook and the West Rim Trail, an hour, no descent.

outings.why: Half a mile of adobe galleries uphill from Paseo de Peralta, then the Museum Hill cluster twenty minutes away by car or a long walk. This is the day that happens inside the town, and it is genuinely good. Most Canyon Road galleries do not o
outings.name: Canyon Road and Museum Hill on foot
outings.season: Year round; Friday evening openings are the best time
outings.fallback: The Plaza, the Palace of the Governors portal and the O'Keeffe Museum, all within four blocks.

destination.name: Northern New Mexico
destination.pitch: Eight days is exactly right for the Rio Grande corridor, because the distances are short, the food is the best in the interior West, and the thousand years of building history along this river is the real subject of the trip.
destination.caveat: Half of what you came to see sits on sovereign land that can close to outsiders on a day's notice for a ceremony, so Taos Pueblo, Acoma, Puye and Tent Rocks all need a phone call the morning of, and Santa Fe itself is expensive and heavily worked over by tourism in a way the rest of the state is not Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.city: Albuquerque is a working city with excellent cheap food and very little to look at, and Santa Fe is a town of 88,000 that behaves like a museum district.
because.food: New Mexican food is its own cuisine, not Tex-Mex and not Mexican, built on two chiles grown in one valley, and the state question at every table is red or green.
because.nature: The Rio Grande cuts an 800 foot basalt gorge north of Taos, the Jemez is the rim of a collapsed supervolcano, and the Chama badlands above Abiquiu are the colours O'Keeffe was accused of exaggerating.
because.culture: Nineteen pueblos, some continuously occupied for 900 years, plus Spanish colonial churches, the Taos and Santa Fe art colonies, and the Manhattan Project, stacked in one valley.
because.adventure: Wheeler Peak, the Kitchen Mesa scramble and the Pueblo Alto rock cleft are honest efforts at altitude, but nothing here is technical or remote in the Alaskan sense.
because.relaxation: Ten Thousand Waves above Santa Fe and the old bath house at Jemez Springs are both real soaks, and an afternoon on a portal at 7,000 feet with nothing scheduled is the correct use of a day here.
because.exploration: Chaco, Bandelier, Tsankawi, Puye and Acoma are five different answers to the same question about how people lived on this plateau, and you can see all five in a week.
